sections.h2: What a small hospital actually needs
paras: A hospital of ten to fifty beds usually runs on a few people doing several jobs each. The same person may handle registration and billing. The pharmacy is one counter. There is no IT department and nobody whose job is to maintain a system. What that hospital needs is the working core done properly: registration under one UHID, OP consultation and prescription, beds and admissions, pharmacy, laboratory and billing including TPA and corporate payers.

What it does not need is an enterprise implementation. Large hospital systems are sold with modules that assume departments you do not have, configuration that assumes staff you cannot spare, and a rollout measured in quarters. HIMS is delivered to a fixed scope, set up with your own data, taught at your own counter, and goes live in 30 working days where the scope allows. Modules you do not run yet are switched on later without starting again.

sections.eyebrow: Why software fails at this size
sections.h2: Small hospitals are sold the wrong problem.
sections.lead: It is rarely the features that defeat a small hospital. It is everything around them.

items.h: Bought for a hospital you are not
items.p: The demo shows department heads, approval chains and roles that assume a staff of hundreds.
The system arrives empty and somebody at the hospital is expected to set up items, rates and users.
One session for whoever was free, then the staff who actually do the work learn from each other.
A counter problem at nine in the morning waits for a response from somebody who has never seen your hospital.
Within a month the billing counter is on the system and everything else has quietly returned to paper.

sections.eyebrow: How a small hospital goes live
sections.h2: From your registers to a working system.

steps.p: We settle what you run today: OP, beds, pharmacy, lab, billing and which payers.
Existing patient, item and rate sheets are brought in rather than retyped.
Departments, doctors, wards, items and users are configured before anyone is trained.
Front desk, pharmacy, ward and billing staff are trained on the screens they will use.
The hospital runs on it, with the founder reachable on WhatsApp during the first weeks.

items.q: Do we need an IT person to run this?
items.a: No. Setup, configuration and data migration are done for you, and training happens at your own counters. Support is on WhatsApp with the founder who built the system, which is the practical answer at this size.

items.q: Can we start with only part of it?
items.a: Yes. Most small hospitals start with registration, OP, pharmacy, beds and billing, then add laboratory, theatre, ICU or the patient portal later. The patient record is the same, so nothing is migrated a second time.

items.q: How quickly can a small hospital switch over?
items.a: The scope is fixed at the start and the target is live in 30 working days where that scope allows. A hospital that wants theatre, ICU and imaging from day one is a larger scope and is quoted as such.
There is no published price, because the scope decides it. Tell us what you run today and how many wards and counters are involved, and the project is scoped on a call.

items.q: We already use a billing package. Is that enough?
items.a: It is enough for bills. It does not hold the clinical record, the beds, the pharmacy stock or the claims, which is where a small hospital loses most of its time. See hospital billing for how billing fits into the whole.
In-person work is Chennai and travel within Tamil Nadu. Everywhere else is served remotely: cloud deployment, remote setup and training, and WhatsApp support. Plenty of hospitals go live that way.

items.p: The whole hospital on one platform.
